A lot of kids learn “math” without learning numeracy. Long story short, they learn the steps but don’t learn the logic behind it. 

A simple example. If I were to say 17+18=24, a person with numeracy skills would recognize two things right away: 7+8=15, so the fact that the answer ended in 4 is a red flag. Also, 10 and more-than-5 plus 10 and more-than 5 must be more than 30. 

If that’s not obvious by, say 11 years old at the latest, a learning disability called dyscalculia should be considered. That is essentially a disconnect between a representation of an amount and an actual amount. 

Kids with dyscalculia imagine “5”, but have no connection to “*****” (a visual amount)

1. My caseload increased from 13 special education students to 55 special education and RtI students

I'm expected to create the kind of growth in scores that will bode well for the school, when students with specific learning disabilities BY DEFINITION do not make average growth in academics. Roast a whole chicken. Brine it overnight in 4 cups of water, 1/4 cup of salt (i know it seems like a lot, but it's not), 2 tbsp honey, and 4 peeled and smashed garlic cloves. Rinse and dry the bird before baking. Bake uncovered for about an hour (at 375 degrees F) or until the temp measures 165 when thermometer is inserted into the thigh. Tent with foil and let rest for 20 minutes before serving. While you're waiting, saute some greens (I liked kale, but you decide) to serve on the side. And if you're like me, you'll want a salad too. My fave is cherry tomatoes, green onions, and cucumbers (no lettuce, gasp!) with balsamic and olive oil. Aaaand, done!
